checkedSources.type: Original paper abstract; the full paper was not read
checkedSources.access: Web tool opened the complete abstract successfully. Direct download returned a cookie challenge, retained and marked as failed content access.
checkedDetails: Eight recognition experiments compared producing words aloud with reading silently.
In the first three experiments, benefits appeared in mixed lists with some words spoken and others read silently.
The abstract proposes that producing words adds distinctive information useful for distinguishing studied items.
checkedSources.readScope: Complete original abstract only. No claim to have read the full paper.
checkedSources.archive: macleod-2010-web-abstract.txt contains the original abstract from the successful web open. production-effect-2010-abstract.html is the direct-download challenge response, not the paper.

checkedSources.type: Original peer-reviewed research PDF hosted by the authors’ university
checkedSources.access: Web PDF and locally saved PDF text checked
checkedDetails: Published in Memory in 2018; first appeared online in 2017.
Ninety-five students began the recording session; 75 returned to complete the study and test session.
Twenty words were assigned to each of four conditions: silent reading, hearing another person, hearing oneself recorded and reading aloud.
The recognition test followed immediately after study; 80 studied words and 80 unstudied words appeared.
Aloud words had the highest mean hit rate. Hearing oneself recorded significantly exceeded hearing another person.
Reading aloud versus hearing oneself recorded yielded p = .08, so the article does not claim an established advantage for that pair.
checkedSources.readScope: Abstract, methods, results, discussion and limitations, printed pages 574–577
checkedSources.uncertainty: The first recording session may have reduced later differences. This experiment measured immediate word recognition rather than general understanding or lifelong memory.

checkedSources.type: Original peer-reviewed research PDF hosted by the authors’ university
checkedSources.access: Web PDF opened; PDF and text saved locally
checkedDetails: Memory & Cognition, 2024, volume 52, pages 57–72; first published online on 13 July 2023.
Four experiments used written passages, with participants reading some passages aloud and others silently.
The study found a consistent advantage for questions focused on memory for the text.
It did not find a consistent advantage for questions requiring broader comprehension.
The first experiment contained weak positive comprehension evidence; later experiments did not confirm it. The article therefore says no consistent benefit, rather than no possible benefit.
checkedSources.readScope: Abstract, scope, first-experiment methods and results, fourth-experiment results and general discussion, especially printed pages 68–69
checkedSources.uncertainty: A distinction in these tasks does not establish an effect for every reader, subject or classroom. No child read-aloud or clinical claim is made.

checkedSources.type: Official institutional history from the college where basketball was invented
checkedSources.access: Web page and saved HTML/text read
checkedDetails: James Naismith devised basketball in 1891.
He wanted two boxes, but the janitor supplied two peach baskets.
He attached them to the lower rail of the gym balcony; the rail happened to be ten feet above the floor.
A man at each end of the balcony retrieved the ball from the basket and returned it to play.
checkedSources.readScope: Full basketball-origin and Naismith history sections, plus the original-rules overview
checkedSources.uncertainty: An attributed institutional historical account. The original artwork will be labelled an imaginative illustration, not an archival photograph or an exact court reconstruction.

checkedSources.access: PDF opened with the web tool, downloaded and extracted with pypdf
checkedDetails: Cover says valid from 1 October 2026.
Section 1.2.4, printed page 9, measures the top edge of the ring at 3,050 mm above the floor, with a maximum tolerance of ±6 mm.
Section 1.2.1 specifies solid steel rings; section 1.3 treats the net separately.
3,050 mm equals 3.05 metres. Ten feet equals 3.048 metres, so approximately ten feet is deliberate.
checkedSources.readScope: Cover, introduction and sections 1.1–1.4, including the exact height clause
checkedSources.discovery: The current official rule index leads to the official resource hub, which links the 2026 equipment v1.0 PDF directly.
checkedSources.uncertainty: This is a FIBA specification. No claim covers every youth, recreational or alternative basketball format.
